rv.q: 'Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown' is far from perfect. But there's enough going on to see this particular glass of gazpacho as half-full.
Welcome to this unsteady but audacious show.
It's not the thin gruel some had feared, but it's also not a spicy knock out — at least not yet.
Your eye will never get weary in a visit to "Women on the Verge," but you're still likely to come out of the experience feeling shortchanged.

Despite a game cast led by the fetching Sherie Rene Scott, this musical adaptation of Pedro Almodovar's 1988 film never finds its footing, lurching between frantic farce and romantic sentiment without achieving a satisfying synthesis.
As a musical, it has no buoyancy, with comedic plot lines deflating in translation and underdeveloped characters scurrying about — often on conveyer belts — without engendering much affection.
Packed with talent and creativity, and a cast and crew bristling with Tony Awards, "Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown" is nonetheless a sad casualty of its own wandering mind.
Despite the insistent beat of David Yazbek’s Spanish-accented score, however, the show can’t find a rhythm.
Bartlett Sher, Theater's resident director, has done his best to make interesting things happen onstage, but the results are scatty and unfocused from start to finish.
The songs themselves are pleasant enough, but they don't advance the plot or develop the characters in meaningful ways, and they frequently stop the show dead in its tracks.
No one is helped by Yazbek's songs, which sound like Latin-flavored Muzak.
But seldom has such a strong cast been used to such poor effect.
Instead, it has turned out to be a hot mess of the highest pedigree.
But what was funny and stylish in the movie is a frantic, unfocused mess here.
But the chief culprits are Lane’s scattershot book and Yazbek’s ho-hum songs, not one of them memorable.
For all its woes, "Women" does stand out in one way.
Fans of the 1988 movie who thought the film would make great sense as a tuner will be baffled at how the skillfully crafted, hilarious flick has deteriorated into such a nearly incoherent shambles.

A yummy confection of silly romantic comedy, seductive Latin music, alluring visuals and high-powered performances, 'Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown' is a musical comedy certain to amuse anyone craving frivolous, tuneful entertainment on Broadway.
Despite its flaws, I still must recommend warmly this musical.
They all try valiantly to rescue this piece of sludge, a show that is so mis-organized that it’s almost like an SAT test to try and re-order the scenes to make the show make sense.

cn.t: Critics pan this musical adaptation as a frantic, incoherent mess that wastes a stellar cast including LuPone, Benanti, and Mitchell. A few praise Laura Benanti's standout performance, but most find it bloated and unfocused.

vs.sum: The Belasco Theatre offers stunning ambiance with its historic Tiffany lamps and stained-glass ceiling, but suffers from tight legroom typical of older venues. While sound quality is generally good, sightlines can be inconsistent, especially from side orchestra seats.
